Why Grief Needs a Second Look

Why Grief Needs a Second Look

1 Sep

Why Grief Needs a Second Look

Beyond stages towards a more relational understanding of loss

Most of us inherit some version of the same map of grief. Loss brings shock, anger and sadness, followed eventually by acceptance. The language varies, but the assumption is familiar: grief follows a progression, and recovery means moving through it.

The appeal is understandable. Loss disorients us; stages give it order. But grief rarely behaves so neatly.

A person can know that someone is no longer and still expect, for a fleeting moment, to hear their voice. Sorrow may recede and return years later. Laughter can appear in the middle of mourning without diminishing the loss. Acceptance, when it comes, does not necessarily mean that grief has finished.

Perhaps we have been asking grief to fit too small a frame.

Loss does not only cause painful feelings. It alters the world in which those feelings arise. The person who has passed away has become part of routines, expectations, relationships, and imagined futures. Their presence is woven into everyday life so completely that much of it goes unnoticed until it is gone.

What disappears, then, is not only a person. A way of living disappears with them.

Grieving is the work of learning to live in the world that remains, and in that process, the relationship itself must change.

Grief may need a different kind of map that helps us understand what loss has changed.

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross’s five-stage model — denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance — remains one of the most familiar ways of talking about grief.

Its origins are often forgotten. Kübler-Ross developed the model through her work with people facing their own deaths. It was later extended into a wider account of bereavement, even though she cautioned that people do not necessarily experience every stage or encounter them in a fixed order. Over time, a description became a script.

Bereavement research does not support the idea that everyone moves through the same emotional sequence. The experiences Kübler-Ross described certainly occur, but in different combinations, at different times and with different intensity.

A model that describes possible responses to loss can therefore unintentionally become a measure of how grief ought to unfold.

The problem is not that the stages contain no truth. It is that a sequence can easily imply a direction. When acceptance appears at the end, it can come to represent where grief is supposed to arrive. Anger, renewed sorrow or a return to earlier feelings may then seem like evidence that someone is not progressing, or has somehow moved backwards.

What the Grieving Brain Has to Learn

Neuroscience offers one part of that picture.

Mary-Frances O’Connor distinguishes between grief and grieving. Grief is the immediate response to loss. Grieving is the longer process through which the brain learns a reality that contradicts years of attachment.

Close relationships are built partly through expectation. We learn where someone will be, how they are likely to respond, and how their presence fits into the rhythm of everyday life. Over time, these expectations become largely automatic.

When someone is no longer with us, the fact may be understood immediately. What has been learned through years of living with them changes more slowly. Some expectations must change. The relationship does not simply disappear with them. Their advice may still influence a decision, their values may have become part of yours, and the way they loved you may continue to shape how you live.

What has to be learned, then, is more complicated than absence. The person is no longer present in the same way.

Grieving involves coming to terms with what has ended while discovering what of the relationship remains.

That discovery does not happen through private thought alone. We make sense of what has changed through the words, images, rituals, and relationships available to us. They give shape to what might otherwise be difficult to say, share, or carry.

How Culture Gives Grief a Language

That work of making sense is never entirely private. We inherit languages, rituals and metaphors that shape how loss can be understood, expressed and shared.

Across cultures, the language of grief often turns towards the body — weight, wounds, illness and pain — and towards relationship: sharing sorrow, remembering, carrying and honouring.

In English, grief is something we describe as heavy; we carry it or feel weighed down by it.

Chinese vocabulary can place sorrow alongside the language of hurt. 悲伤 (bēishāng), for example, draws together sadness and injury.

Japanese traditions include mono no aware, an attentiveness to the poignancy of impermanence.

The Vietnamese condolence phrase chia buồn expresses the idea of sharing another person’s sadness.

Thai and Khmer words derived from Sanskrit and Pali śoka sit within long traditions of reflection on suffering, loss and impermanence.

These examples do not explain how whole cultures grieve. They show something more modest: people have long reached beyond an inner vocabulary of emotion to speak about loss. Culture gives grief forms through which it can be recognised by others and held in common.

Yet language and ritual can only take us so far. Loss does not only alter what a person feels or how they speak about it. It can alter the world in which their life once made sense.

When a Lived World Breaks

Neuroscience can describe how expectations change. It cannot fully capture what happens when the familiar world to which those expectations belonged no longer holds.

Philosopher and psychiatrist Thomas Fuchs describes grief as a disruption of the lived world: the largely taken-for-granted web of habits, relationships and assumptions through which everyday life makes sense. Before a loss, a person does not think, My partner will still be here today. They simply live in a world in which that is true.

After death, much may look unchanged. But the world organised around that person is not. Roles shift. Responsibilities change. Familiar places carry different meanings.

Because identity is partly formed in relationship, grief can also unsettle the sense of who one is. Bereavement, therefore, asks more than “How do I live without this person?”

It can also ask: “Who am I now, in a world where they are no longer here?”

That is why grief can feel larger than sadness. Loss can alter the very structure through which life once made sense.

Once the familiar world has been disrupted, the question is not simply how to restore it. It is about understanding and living within what has changed.

Meaning After Loss

Meaning matters here, but not because every loss contains a lesson or eventually reveals a purpose. Some deaths remain senseless, unjust or difficult to reconcile.

Meaning-making is not about turning suffering into something positive. It is about finding some way for what has happened to become part of a life that can still be lived.

The question may not be “What good can come from this?“ It may simply be: “How do I understand my life now that this has happened?”

Viktor Frankl placed meaning at the centre of his understanding of suffering. Contemporary bereavement research approaches similar territory through ideas such as sense-making and meaning reconstruction.

The meanings we make, however, do not always help. Meaning can sustain us, but it can also deepen suffering. This is because loss can unsettle assumptions that previously helped us make sense of life — about who we are, what we can rely on, how relationships endure, or what we imagined the future would be like.

When those assumptions no longer hold, some rethinking becomes unavoidable. A person has to work out, consciously or otherwise, what has changed, what still remains true, and how this loss now belongs within the life they continue to live.

The task is therefore not simply to feel better. It is to make a changed reality sufficiently intelligible that life can be lived within it again.

This work has always involved memory, story, ritual, and the continuing influence of the person who is gone. Digital technology is beginning to change the materials through which that work now takes place.

Grief in the Digital Age

Technology introduces a new complication to continuing bonds.

The dead have always remained with us through memories, stories, photographs, rituals and the values we carry forward. Digital media has made many of these traces more persistent. Artificial intelligence introduces something different: representations of the dead can now respond.

If grieving involves learning how a relationship continues after physical reciprocity has ended, what happens when technology begins to simulate that reciprocity?

We do not yet know what this will mean for grief. Questions about memory, presence and the changing boundary between remembrance and relationship deserve an article of their own.

For now, the important point is that technology is beginning to change not only how we remember the dead, but what it may mean to maintain a continuing bond.

Towards a Better Map of Grief

A better map of grief does not replace one sequence with another. It begins from a different premise: loss changes both the world a person inhabits and the relationship that helped give that world its meaning.

The questions therefore change. Not Which stage am I in? or When should this be over? but,

What has changed? What now has to be learned? What can continue, and in what form?

These are not steps towards an endpoint. They allow for adaptation without demanding detachment, continuing bonds without denying death, and meaning without requiring suffering to become a lesson.

As culture and technology reshape how we remember, relate and live with absence, these distinctions will matter even more.

Grief may never become orderly. But our understanding of it can become more adequate — able to hold together absence and connection, finality and enduring significance.

Death is final. The relationship changes with it, but is not necessarily erased.

Grieving is learning how both can be true: They are gone, and they still matter.
